title: HEIF Heist- Hacking OpenAI, Slack, Meta, GitHub and Many Others
content:
What is HEIF Heist?
A bug that could have allowed us to
- Dump of OpenAI private repositories
- RCE on Slack which allows leaking files
- RCE in Meta's core product suite via image upload
- Leak arbitrary Redacted users' tokens, and AWS access tokens
- Authenticated RCE on Discourse
- Unauthenticated RCE in Next.js via AVIF Image Optimization
- Authenticated RCE on GitHub Enterprise (CVE-2026-19118)
- RCE on multiple web frameworks/cms.
- Leak user's files, and sensitive info from multiple applications.
HEIF Heist is Hacktron's name for a class of remote attack paths targeting services that decode attacker-controlled HEIF, HEIC, or AVIF images. By exploiting underlying native libraries, these vulnerabilities allow an attacker to bypass application-level defenses and trigger memory corruption, data exposure, or remote code execution (RCE).
The vulnerable attack surface lives below the application layer inside native C/C++ decoders such as libheif and libde265. These parsers typically enter production environments indirectly bundled via higher-level wrappers like ImageMagick, libvips, or Sharp, standard distro packages, and prebuilt container base images.
By probing upload endpoints with crafted .avif or .heic files, an attacker can fingerprint the remote libheif version family in use. Once identified, they can fire an exact version-matched n-day or 0-day payload to trigger memory corruption, data exfiltration, or remote code execution.
Research origin
HEIF Heist began as part of the Hacktron research team's broader security research into frontier labs. After discovering and reporting a libheif RCE in Discourse, we asked a larger question: how many other applications depend on the same image-processing stack?
Past vulnerabilities such as ImageTragick, ForcedEntry, and the libwebp flaw have demonstrated the reach of an image processor or parser vulnerability. An image parser might generate an operating-system thumbnail or process a web upload, giving it an enormous blast radius.
That initial finding grew into a multi-month investigation tracing libheif across communication platforms, cloud services, enterprise products, and popular web frameworks.
FAQ
Why is it called HEIF Heist?
Even when Remote Code Execution (RCE) isn't immediately achievable, the attack primitives may still allow arbitrary heap disclosure, letting an attacker “heist” in-memory data such as other users' data and environment variables.
What makes it unique?
The vulnerability sits inside native C/C++ parsers (libheif / libde265), making it completely language and framework-agnostic. Any backend processing untrusted user image uploads is potentially exposed to these parsers.
What versions are affected, and how do I fix it?
HEIF Heist is not tied to a single version. It targets an entire ecosystem of vulnerabilities across multiple release families (e.g. 1.19.x, 1.20.x, 1.22.x, 1.23.x). Any deployment lacking the latest upstream security patches is potentially vulnerable.
- Update upstream. Upgrading to libheif v1.23.2 or later and the latestlibde265 , via your distribution's security channel or a direct source build, is recommended to patch known 0-day and n-day vectors.
- Defense in depth. Given the complexity of the ISO base media file format and the pace of decoder updates, future memory-safety flaws are likely. Production architectures should disable untrusted HEIF/AVIF decoding where it is not needed, or isolate image-processing pipelines inside hardened, ephemeral sandboxes.
Separately, if you self-host Discourse or Next.js, ensure you are on the latest release and follow their security advisories.
Is it easy to exploit?
These are not out-of-the-box exploits. Exploitation requires fingerprinting the target version and tailoring the payload image(s). Some of our RCE attempts landed only after thousands of image uploads. That said, an AI agentic approach with a frontier model like GPT-5.6 Sol cut exploit development time down to roughly 1 to 3 days from initial probe to remote RCE. A motivated attacker can convert a vulnerable upload endpoint into RCE or an info leak.
Who found it?
Led by Harsh Jaiswal, alongside Mohan SRK, Rahul Maini, and Sudhanshu Rajbhar from the Hacktron research team, assisted by Hacktron Harness, GPT-5.6 Sol, and Opus 5.
Work with the team behind this research.
Hacktron brings together top CTF researchers, experienced red teamers, and offensive security researchers. We use AI to accelerate security research, finding and eliminating vulnerabilities in widely trusted software before malicious actors do. We're continuing our research across frontier labs and other internet-critical systems. If you're responsible for securing one of them, we'd like to work with you.

report.summary: Hacktron researchers disclose "HEIF Heist," a class of image-decoder flaws letting attackers breach OpenAI, Slack, Meta, GitHub and others via malicious HEIF/AVIF uploads.
report.background: Image parsers have a long history of outsized blast radius: ImageTragick in ImageMagick, Apple's ForcedEntry, and the 2023 libwebp flaw each turned a single decoder bug into mass compromise. HEIF Heist extends that lineage to the HEIF/HEIC/AVIF family. The vulnerable code lives below the application layer, in native C/C++ libraries such as libheif and libde265, which reach production indirectly through ImageMagick, libvips, Sharp, distro packages, and prebuilt container images. The Hacktron team started from an RCE they found and reported in Discourse's libheif usage, then asked how many other services share that stack. Over months they traced the dependency across communication platforms, cloud services, enterprise products, and web frameworks. Crucially, the exploits are not turnkey: they require first fingerprinting the target's remote libheif version via crafted uploads, then tailoring version-matched n-day or 0-day payloads.
key_points: The attack surface sits in native C/C++ decoders (libheif, libde265) rather than in application code, making the flaws language- and framework-agnostic. Any backend that accepts untrusted image uploads — whether Node, Python, Ruby, or Go — is potentially exposed if a vulnerable decoder is bundled somewhere in its image pipeline.

Reported targets include a dump of OpenAI private repositories, RCE and file leakage on Slack, RCE in Meta's core product suite via image upload, token and AWS credential leakage from Redacted, authenticated RCE on Discourse, unauthenticated RCE in Next.js via AVIF optimization, and authenticated RCE on GitHub Enterprise (CVE-2026-19118).

Even when full RCE is not achievable, the primitives can yield arbitrary heap disclosure, letting an attacker "heist" in-memory data such as other users' content, secrets, and environment variables. The name HEIF Heist comes directly from this data-exfiltration angle.

Fingerprinting is the first step: attackers probe upload endpoints with crafted .avif or .heic files to identify the remote libheif version family, then fire an exact version-matched payload. Affected families span 1.19.x, 1.20.x, 1.22.x and 1.23.x, so fixes are not tied to a single release.

Weaponization is getting cheaper through AI. The team says an agentic approach with a frontier model like GPT-5.6 Sol compressed exploit development from probe to remote RCE to roughly one to three days, though some attempts still needed thousands of crafted uploads to land.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a pointed reminder that frontier labs and SaaS platforms inherit risk from decades-old C image code, not just from their own models or APIs. For developers, the practical consequence is that "we only accept image uploads" is not a safe position: the decoder behind that upload endpoint is part of the attack surface, and self-hosted projects like Discourse and Next.js need prompt patching and advisory tracking. For regular users, the exposure is indirect but real — account tokens, AWS credentials, private repositories, and other users' files can leak without any obvious warning. The longer-term shift is architectural: teams are being pushed toward sandboxing, re-encoding images, or disabling HEIF/AVIF decoding where it is not strictly required.
report.tools: Follow libheif (upgrade to v1.23.2 or later) and libde265 on your distro's security channel. Audit your image pipeline: ImageMagick, libvips, and Sharp all bundle these decoders, and prebuilt container base images often lag. Check Discourse and Next.js security advisories if you self-host. For defense in depth, run image processing in hardened ephemeral sandboxes (gVisor, Firecracker, seccomp/jail restrictions), disable unused HEIF/AVIF decoding, and re-encode untrusted uploads server-side. Track Hacktron's forthcoming technical write-ups for fingerprints and PoC details.
